claims.text: Four statutes, each with a different addressee. DoD: 10 U.S.C. 119 (defense committees; annual 1 Mar; waiver in (e) collapsing to chairman + ranking member). NNSA: 50 U.S.C. 2426 (congressional defense committees; annual 1 Feb; identical waiver). All other non-IC agencies: 50 U.S.C. 3348 (congressional oversight committees; annual 1 Feb; waiver that does NOT reduce the audience). IC: 50 U.S.C. 3091a (intelligence committees + both Appropriations + the four congressional leaders; semiannual briefings; no waiver at all).

The seams are written into the statutes. 50 U.S.C. 3348(g)(2)(B) removes DoD, NNSA and every IC element from its own coverage. 50 U.S.C. 3091a(d)(3) defines its subject by reference to ICD 906. ICD 906 section C.3 in turn removes from its own coverage every SAP created by the Secretaries of State, Defense, Energy or Homeland Security or the Attorney General, and 'special access programs under the purview of the National Security Council, such as covert action.'

Composed, the four regimes leave two seams with no annual census obligation running to a full committee: (i) a DoD program under a 119(e) waiver, whose content goes only to chairs and ranking members and whose annual report requirement additionally sunset on 31 Dec 2021 under Pub. L. 114-328 sec. 1061; and (ii) anything protected by ACCM rather than SAP controls, which no statute names. Covert action under 50 U.S.C. 3093 is a third, separately governed channel. Reasoning stated from the four statutes plus 32 CFR 117.3.
Four separate statutes govern SAP-type reporting: 10 U.S.C. 119 (DoD), 50 U.S.C. 2426 (NNSA), 50 U.S.C. 3348 (all other non-IC agencies) and 50 U.S.C. 3091a (IC controlled access programs).

claims.source: Comparison of 10 U.S.C. 119(e), 50 U.S.C. 2426(e), 50 U.S.C. 3348(e) and 50 U.S.C. 3091a
claims.text: Of the four regimes, only 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) and 50 U.S.C. 2426(e)(2) narrow the recipient of waived information to the chairman and ranking minority member; 50 U.S.C. 3348(e)(2) keeps the full oversight committees, and 50 U.S.C. 3091a has no waiver provision at all.
Only 50 U.S.C. 3091a carries a funding prohibition tied to notification, added by section 6602 of Public Law 118-159 on 23 December 2024.

A program moved between the DoD and IC regimes changes both its governing statute and its reporting audience, and before 23 December 2024 no statute required notice of the move. That is a documented, lawful, unnotified route by which a program's oversight history can be broken. Reasoning: the prohibition added by Pub. L. 118-159 sec. 6603 did not exist before that date and operates prospectively.

connections.label: Alternative Compensatory Control Measures (ACCM)
connections.note: ACCM is the hole in the map. 32 CFR 117.23 places it in the same regulated set as SAPs, SCI, RD, FRD, TFNI and NNPI, and names it first in the heading - but it is the only member of that set with no reporting statute attached. 10 U.S.C. 119, 50 U.S.C. 2426, 3348 and 3091a each key on 'special access program' or 'controlled access program'. A measure that is neither falls outside all four.

desc: There is no single United States statute on special access programs. There are four parallel regimes plus covert action, and the differences between them are where a program can live. (1) DoD - 10 U.S.C. 119: annual report by 1 March, new-program notice by 1 February, 14-day declassification notice, 30-day report-and-wait, all to six defense committees; the Secretary may waive the reports on a national-security determination, in which case the information goes only to the chairman and ranking minority member of each. (2) NNSA - 50 U.S.C. 2426: identical structure to the defense committees, but the Administrator may additionally waive the 30-day report-and-wait itself. (3) Every other agency - 50 U.S.C. 3348: identical structure, but reporting runs to 'congressional oversight committees' expressly including House Oversight and Senate Homeland Security, and the waiver does not narrow the audience. (4) The Intelligence Community - 50 U.S.C. 3091a and ICD 906: no annual statutory deadline and no waiver at all, but semiannual briefings on every program, a prohibition on establishment before notification, a funding cutoff since December 2024, and a prohibition on transferring capabilities out of a CAP into a SAP without notice since December 2024. Set beside each other, the ranking is unambiguous: the weakest reporting regime in the United States government belongs to the Department of Defense, and it is weakest precisely at the point where the Secretary decides how much to tell the committees. Two structural seams follow. The first is between regimes: a capability transferred from an IC controlled access program to a DoD special access program changes which statute governs it and which committees see it - the manoeuvre Congress prohibited prospectively in December 2024, three decades after the alleged conduct. The second is around all four: ICD 906 section C.3 records that none of them applies to 'special access programs under the purview of the National Security Council, such as covert action', which are governed only by 50 U.S.C. 3093 and its Gang of Eight.

entityInfo.desc: Where a program could sit, and what changes when it moves. There are five distinct legal environments, and the practical differences between them are the map of where concealment is easiest. (1) A DoD special access program: reports to six defense committees, waivable to eight to twelve members by the Secretary's own determination. (2) An NNSA special access program: same committees, and the Administrator may additionally waive the 30-day advance notice itself, so a program can begin with no committee ever having been told in advance - and NNSA material is Restricted Data, born classified by operation of the Atomic Energy Act rather than by an original classification authority, so a presidential declassification order operating on E.O. 13526 information does not reach it. (3) A non-DoD, non-NNSA, non-IC agency special access program: reports to House Oversight and Senate Homeland Security among others, and the waiver does not narrow the audience - the strongest of the SAP regimes, and the one covering DHS, NASA, Justice and Commerce. (4) An IC Controlled Access Program: no waiver at all, semiannual briefings, a funding cutoff since December 2024 and, since December 2024, a prohibition on transferring a capability out into a special access program without notice. (5) A National Security Council covert action program: outside all four SAP regimes by the express terms of ICD 906 section C.3, governed only by 50 U.S.C. 3093. The seam that matters is between (4) and (1). Before 23 December 2024 there was no statutory requirement to notify anyone when a capability moved from an IC controlled access program into a DoD special access program, and the move changes both the governing statute and the committees entitled to know. Congress closed that door prospectively in section 6603 of Public Law 118-159 - and left it ajar with an exception for transfers 'necessary to maintain access in the event of an organizational restructuring', a determination the transferring official makes for himself.
